title: Host Software
summary: One of the very first Network Working Group notes, dated April 1969. It sketches how the ARPANET's message processors (IMPs) work and what software the connected host computers would need in order to talk to one another. It also lists open questions and proposes some early experiments. It is a discussion paper, not a specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1 describes early ideas for software that would let ARPANET host computers communicate. It summarizes the network's message processors and proposes ways for hosts to open connections, transfer files and handle terminal input.

subtitle: A tentative 1969 sketch of how ARPANET hosts could exchange messages and establish connections.

tldr.problem: The IMP software had been specified, but the connected host computers still needed to agree on their own communication software.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC summarizes IMP messages and links, then proposes host operations for interactive and file-like connections and local handling of terminal input.
tldr.outcome: The author says very little is firm. The memo presents open questions and two initial experiments rather than a final specification.

sections.title: A Tentative Host Software Proposal
sections.content:
The ARPA Network's software was split between the Interface Message Processors (IMPs) and the connected host computers. BBN had specified the IMP software, while the host groups needed to agree on host software. Steve Crocker presents tentative agreements and open questions from discussions among the early network sites.

The RFC says very little of its proposal is firm and asks readers for reactions. It also lists initial experiments planned around the SRI online retrieval system.
sections.plainLanguage: The network's message processors had been specified, but the attached computers still needed common software rules. This memo shares early ideas and asks for comments.

sections.title: Messages, Links and Packets
sections.content:
Hosts exchange messages of up to 8080 bits plus a 16-bit header. The header contains a destination, link, trace flag and spare bits. The trace flag asks the IMPs to record message status and send it to the Network Measurement Center at UCLA.

Each host pair has 32 logical full-duplex links. A host must wait for a Request for Next Message (RFNM) from the destination IMP before sending another message on the same link. An IMP divides messages into packets of at most 1010 bits, adds a 24-bit cyclic checksum, and reassembles packets at the destination.
sections.plainLanguage: The network divides host messages into packets and checks them during transmission. A host also waits for an acknowledgment before sending another message on the same link.

sections.title: Connections and Local Terminal Handling
sections.content:
The proposal reserves link 0 for communication between host operating systems and uses the other 31 links for user connections. To establish a connection, one host asks over link 0 and the other accepts. If both choose the same link at once, a priority rule makes one host select a different free link.

For large transfers, programs can establish a separate file-like connection alongside a terminal-like connection. The RFC also proposes a console-control language called DEL. A host could run a local front-end program to handle simple keystrokes and send a completed line to the remote host, reducing delay from individual remote responses.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal uses a control link to set up separate connections for interactive use and large transfers. It also suggests handling simple typing locally before sending input across the network.
